[[RunningHead]]

Commentary on “Becoming Aware of Feelings”

Robert Galatzer-Levy

Robert Galatzer-Levy

Chicago

Robert Galatzer-Levy  

Ever since Breuer (in Freud, 1895) observed that Anna O.'s symptoms remitted when she remembered the circumstances of their onset with affect, analysts have struggled with the problem of emotion. Clearly, emotions are of central importance in people's psychological lives, but they are not easily encompassed in the vocabulary developed to describe cognitive function, or even ordinary discursive speech. As a result, much analytic discourse about emotions follows Breuer's lead in treating emotions as a kind of attachment to cognition. Even though the concept of signal anxiety (Freud, 1926) provided some means for conceptualizing emotions in a way more related to information processing, much psychoanalytic discussion of emotion continued Freud's early hydraulic view of emotion as a quantifiable substance that followed conservation laws similar to the laws of the conservation of mass and energy (Galatzer-Levy, 1976). This approach found further support in the description of traumatic states as involving some sort of quantitative overwhelming of the psychological apparatus. Both these ideas, despite their clearly fantastical nature, found favor, in part because they corresponded well to many people's subjective experience of emotion. They fit particularly well with the fantasies of ridding oneself of distressing emotions by placing them somewhere else (e.g. in another person) that were described by Melanie Klein and her followers. Despite strenuous efforts by analysts to develop more adequate conceptualizations of emotion, analytic practice to this day is largely dominated by the same metaphors that Freud used in his early formulations.

Matters are further complicated because analysts often use the term “affect” to refer to a variety of matters that are difficult to include in ordinary discursive discourse. In this view, the mental world is divided into cognition and affect. Sometimes an additional area of “unconscious fantasy”—which functions by different rules but in a manner similar to ordinary cognition—is also included in these discussions. However, the detailed description of mental processes that are fundamentally dissimilar from ordinary cognition and are of the greatest importance to psychological function has only seen a limited development by way of the works of Wilfred Bion (1977) and his followers. Psychoanalytic discourse about emotion and affect often becomes confused because it includes a large group of mental processes that have nothing in common except their divergence from rational discourse.

Response to Commentaries

Richard Lane and David Garfield

David Garfield

David Garfield  

The purpose of our target article was to lay the foundation for a comprehensive theory of how the forms and transformations of affect are at the heart of the therapeutic mechanism of change in psychoanalysis. In our view, many important and salient points have been raised by this distinguished group of commentators. We view their comments, for the most part, as raising issues that will need to be addressed as the basic template that we outlined in the target paper gets filled in and then incorporated into mainstream psychoanalytic theory and practice. In the pages that follow, we explain why we hold this position, and what bridges will need to be built between what we have presented and other conceptual frameworks. We believe that this will result in the creation of a comprehensive theory of clinical change, with affect at its core. We begin by making general remarks and then address the specific issues raised by each commentator.

Our starting point for our target article is that the fundamental problems that bring patients in for psychoanalytic treatment involve emotional responses that are out of conscious awareness. We believe that emotional change in psychoanalysis can occur in two ways—with emotional awareness and without it. Our target article focused on the former and, in a secondary way, outlined the latter. The fundamental process of change with insight involves bringing these emotions into awareness, understanding the meaning of these emotions, and then using this understanding to change how one navigates the external world. We wish to emphasize that this fundamental principle was not challenged by any of the commentators. The important issues that they raised involve how one conceptualizes that process and exactly what neural structures are involved as the transformations occur.

The commentators who responded most favorably, and appeared to accept our conceptualization most fully, were Dr. Leslie Greenberg from the perspective of psychotherapy and Dr. Michael Posner from the perspective of neuroscience. Greenberg is unusual in that he has created a form of psychotherapy that is emotion-focused and is empirically based using objective methodologies. Although not formally psychoanalytic, his approach is broadly consistent with psychoanalytic principles. Posner is the only cognitive neuroscientist among the commentators but, nevertheless, is one who has made very important contributions to the field, including the study of emotion regulation from a developmental perspective. Thus, two very highly regarded investigators, who work within very different disciplines, find that our model is consistent with existing knowledge in each of their domains and that it provides a useful integration of the two. Thus, we have achieved a synthesis of cognitive neuro-scientific understanding of the processing of emotion in the brain on the one hand, and an established form of psychotherapy that focuses on emotion and is supported by empirical research on the other. We believe that achieving a synthesis of this kind should not be taken lightly. To our knowledge, no other synthesis of this kind exists.

Ongoing Discussion

Douglas F. Watt's Book Review of Lane & Nadel, Cognitive Neuroscience of Emotion

Richard Lane and Lynn Nadel

Lynn Nadel

Tucson

Lynn Nadel  

A review of Cognitive Neuroscience of Emotion (Lane & Nadel, 2000) was published in this journal several years ago. The review, though generally favorable, criticized our first chapter and the title of the book. These argued that emotion can profitably be studied within the domain of cognitive neuroscience and that a separate field of affective neuroscience is unnecessary. Since the current target article is an expression of this new approach to emotion and is an elaboration of one of the chapters in the book (chapter 15), it seemed important to address comments from the review and, where possible, correct any misconceptions that the review may have generated.

A central thesis of the book is that purely psychological approaches can be transformed when integrated with neuroscientific knowledge. The field of neuro-psychoanalysis, for example, has been created based on the belief that understanding neural processes will inform and refine the practice of psychoanalysis. In a related manner, we believe that neurobiological understanding calls into question the traditional distinction between cognition and emotion, which became entrenched with Descartes. In recent years there has been a growing appreciation of the adaptive usefulness of emotion that emanates from the tradition of Darwin. The seminal work of Damasio and colleagues on ventromedial prefrontal cortex has affirmed that strict distinctions between emotion and cognition may no longer be valid (Damasio, 1994).

With the discovery of implicit cognitive functions, cognition can no longer be equated with conscious thought, and the boundary used to define what is and what is not cognitive has become obscure. As we describe in the first chapter of the book, cognition can now be more broadly defined as information processing. As such, emotion is also cognitive in the sense that its various components involve information processing. Traditional distinctions between emotion and cognition therefore break down when it is considered that cognitive processes can be embodied (e.g. learned procedures), can have autonomic concomitants, and may not be conscious. Indeed, others have begun to adopt this cognitive neuroscientific perspective on emotion, such as in the upcoming target article in Behavioral and Brain Sciences by Lewis (in press) entitled “Bridging Emotion Theory and Neurobiology through Dynamic Systems Modeling.” In that paper neurobiological evidence is presented in support of the view that emotion and cognition are not two distinct systems and that the cognitive antecedents and the cognitive consequences of emotion are one and the same.

Iréne Matthis  

During the year 2004 the group has initiated two main activities: the first was the creation of a new professional course for a diploma of Psychosomatics at the University of Paris 8. It is centered on the interdisciplinary field of psychoanalysis, neuroscience, and medicine, and the training is formulated to suit medical doctors, psychotherapists, and psychoanalysts. The teaching staff consists of 19 members, among whom are professors of medicine and doctors of the hospital La Pitié-Salpêtrière, where all the courses are taught. Jean Benjamin Stora is pedagogical and scientific director, and 7 members of the French group belong to the staff. Mark Solms is a member of the scientific diploma committee. It is a 1-year course offering 120 hours of classes and 150 hours of internship at the medical department of the hospital. The first course started in November 2004, and 14 students have registered for the new program.

The second main activity of the group has been our monthly seminars. In September 2004 we discussed the topic of “feminine sexuality and processes of somatiza-tion.” Based on a rereading of Sigmund Freud's lecture on femininity (1931), Jean Benjamin Stora developed the metapsychological model underlying the psychosexual development of women.

[[RunningHead]]

Commentary on “Integrating the Psychoanalytic and Neurobiological Views of Panic Disorder”

David Pincus

David Pincus

Cleveland, Ohio

David Pincus  

Alexander, Feigelson, & Gorman have sought to create a bridge between varying perspectives on panic disorder. The anchoring for one side of the bridge is the post-1926 psychoanalytic structural model, and the anchor from the other side of the bridge is a series of observations from the neuroscientific literature which center around the amygdala and its relationships to other brain structures and activities. The span is offered in the form of classical conditioning, whereby psychoanalytic and neuroscientific constructs can be understood within a conditioning paradigm, and panic and anxiety disorders can be more richly elucidated within this paradigm. The authors state: “We are proposing a theoretical overlap between classical conditioning and the psychodynamic theory of panic disorder”. Classical conditioning has also been used extensively to study fear conditioning in the neurosciences. “We postulate that classical conditioning could serve as a link between the psychodynamic and neurobiological understanding of anxiety.” Beyond the grand effort of an integration, the authors do provide us with a summary of important findings of the functioning of the amygdala and an interesting review of classical conditioning. Others can comment upon the amygdalocentric focus in the authors' analysis of the neurobiological research; I shall attend more to matters of integrating.

Integrating models and clinical strategies have the benefit of informing novel clinical interventions and research programs from neighboring disciplines. Several authors over the past 30 years have sought to bring analytic thought into closer proximity to conditioning models, such as the work of Wachtel (1981) and Cooper (1992). It has been proposed by many that the transference-countertransference working through in the analytic process is a form of exposure and extinguishing of traumatic memories, relearning new possible outcomes to feared situations, and unlearning failed strategies of the past. For the process to succeed, the problematic past becomes manifest though is not entirely repeated in the clinical encounter, and the safety and insight of the new experience allow for a new integration and more flexible ways of learning and experiencing. Within psychoanalysis itself, the therapeutic interaction has been viewed in a similar way, though without such an explicit emphasis upon a learning paradigm. Thus, corrective emotional experiences, and mastering and controlling stimuli and meanings by the ego, are two trends within psychoanalysis that speak to the issue of new learning, unlearning, or relearning.

Steven Ellman , Bonnie Smolen and Douglas Watt

Douglas Watt

email: Sellman174@aol.com

Douglas Watt  

Mark J. Blechner has put forth an interesting perspective on dream life in his new volume The Dream Frontier. Blechner attempts not only a view of dreams and dreaming, but on occasion moves into contemporary neuroscience, exploring theories of consciousness, processes of decision making, and the underlying mechanisms of certain neurological conditions. The main focus of his work, however, is a running commentary on Freud's dream theory, alongside his own views of how the dream appears in the clinical situation. He relates not only how an analyst might receive, interpret, and perhaps even create a patient's dream, but also how the dream may be presented in the supervisory process. Given all that he attempts, his book must in some ways fall short, since no one author can cover all this material in a single 300-page book. To be more specific, in reading Blechner's book I would say that in each of his 22 chapters I found something that I strongly disagreed with, but I also found each of his chapters interesting and stimulating. I was appreciative of the amount of work that has gone into the excellent integration of material from areas that do not obviously fit together. In my initial attempt at this review, I did not clearly state Blechner's theoretical orientation. Rather—as is true of Blechner himself (at least in this volume)—I implied that his position, while usually respectful of Freud, attempts to show how an approach that veers towards the manifest content of the dream can both be helpful to the analytic clinician and explain phenomena garnered from laboratory studies. It is a position that subtly instructs the clinician to value more highly the narrative as it appears in the dream report (using the term “manifest content” already imposes a theoretical bias). It seems to me that Blechner is interested in the dream as a creation that can be distilled for the patient. Thus, Harry Stack Sullivan's (and Jung's) technique of dream distillation is highly valued by Blechner. Sullivan's technique seems to me to attempt to get at the relevant emotional content of the dream and express it directly to the patient. Thus, when a patient presents a dream of a Dutch windmill with a beautiful scene on the outside of the windmill and wrack and ruin on the inside, Sullivan comments, “That is beautiful, active on the outside—utterly dead and decayed within” (quoted by Blechner, p. 137). Blechner implies that although Sullivan scorned Freud's idea of latent content, in the dream he was able to reach latent content quite directly through his technique of distillation. This example is indicative of Blechner's attempt to blend different theoretical positions while moving the center of a dream theory more towards the dream as reported and experienced.

Alexandre Métraux  

According to the OED, “crosswise” means, among other things, either “with one crossing another, alternately” or “across, athwart, transversely.” The advantage of reading crosswise (but not athwart) two books that address closely related topics is that either text may thrillingly complement the other in the reader's mind. The disadvantage of reading crosswise, however, is that, like in cross-breeding, the originality and/or self-sufficiency of either entity may partly get blurred in the reader's mind. In what follows, I shall try to take advantage of reviewing crosswise two monographs on neuro-psychoanalysis, without distorting too much the uniqueness of either book considered independently from the other. It is thus fair to indicate first what the books under review are about.

The monograph by Karen Kaplan-Solms and Mark Solms (Clinical Studies, for short) consists of three parts. Part I contains a chapter on the historical origins of psychoanalysis in neuroscience, a chapter on Aleksandr Luria, a chapter on the neuro-psychoanalysis of dreaming, and a chapter on the future of neuro-psychoanalysis. Part II is devoted to clinical observations of cases that illustrate what neuro-psychoanalysis is (among other things): (1) an ensemble of methods that are likely to disclose some emotional and cognitive alterations in one's life caused by brain injuries (alterations that are usually not dealt with in cognitive neuroscience); (2) a means by which some psychoanalytic theorems are put to test; and (3) a set of more or less formal interaction patterns, both observational and therapeutic, adapted to the physical and psychological conditions of brain-injured patients. And part III, which consists of just one chapter, sketches the neuroanatomy of the mental apparatus, thus knotting together the various threads running through the previous chapters.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Commentary on “Becoming Aware of Feelings”

Leslie Greenberg PHD

Leslie Greenberg

Toronto

Leslie Greenberg  

“Emotion, which is suffering, ceases to be suffering as soon as we form a clear and precise picture of it.”

Spinoza, Ethics(1967)

In their paper, Lane & Garfield present a cogent argument that elaborates on the above quotation from Spinoza. The authors develop the idea that the conscious awareness of emotion involves a domain of cognition separate from that of other cognitive processes, and that this emotional awareness has a therapeutic effect on patients who become conscious of their own emotions. They offer a developmental and modulatory perspective on the emergence of conscious aspects of emotion. The key proposition in their cognitive-developmental theory is that knowledge is transformed from implicit (i.e. procedural and sensory) to explicit (i.e. conscious thought) representation through the use of language and symbol. Lane's LEAS describes the move from implicit to explicit emotional experience in a number of stages. These stages involve the progressive differentiation of sensory and procedural emotional experience into more complex conscious symbolization of self-emotion and, at the highest level, integration of awareness of emotion of self and other.

They support this view with strong neuroscientific evidence. Focusing on vertical relations in the medial systems in the brain, they review evidence showing that cortical participation is necessary for emotional experience, and they argue that neural substrates of implicit and explicit emotional processes are dissociable. The amygdala has been shown to respond to stimuli in the absence of conscious awareness of the stimuli: it operates implicitly and is cognitively impenetrable. The authors then show that cortical participation is necessary for emotional experience, and they present impressive evidence from their own laboratory that implicates the ventral and dorsal anterior cingulate cortices in awareness of both background feelings and focal attention to feelings. They emphasize, however, that the latter area of the brain is specific not to emotion but, rather, to attention. They then claim that reflective awareness, dependent on dorsomedial pre-frontal cortex, also involves an area not specific to emotion.

Response

Douglas Watt

Douglas Watt

Douglas Watt  

I appreciate very much the comments by Drs. Lane and Nadel on the book review of Cognitive Neuroscience of Emotion published in Neuro-Psychoanalysis in 2001. However, after considering their comments, I am not entirely sure that we have clarified the issues that we might agree, or disagree, on. It is always a challenge to represent the views of colleagues accurately, and I certainly would not want to distort their views in any critique, and thus “‘knock down a straw man’.” I appreciate several of their clarifications, and perhaps in the end it is a matter of emphasis rather than profound conceptual differences. However, I still feel that there is a fundamentally different emphasis between us, in terms of advocacy for the notion that virtually all of the core, and particularly the more primitive, components of emotion can be classed as cognitive. Are valence, the intrinsically pleasurable or unpleasurable nature of emotion, motivational drive, and the global CNS arousal associated with strong emotion all fundamentally cognitive? If they are, then it seems to me that one has basically expanded the notion of cognition to annex everything that has traditionally been considered core to emotion. If so, then what is left? And if this is the basic set of definitions and assumptions, isn't this a radically expanded notion of cognition?

The problem of making cognition and emotion virtually completely equivalent (as the Editors in the reviewed volume appeared, in many places, to do) is that it goes against any assumption of evolutionary

progression or phylogenetic extension—in which cognitive processing comes to differentially modulate, activate, and inhibit emotion, while emotion directs, gates, and motivates all cognitive processing. Fully analogously, emotion anticipates potential homeostatic demand and challenge. However, this does not mean that homeostasis can be considered “the same as emotion.”

I worry that the cognitive neuroscience of emotion, if it believes that it can somehow “annex” emotion and turn it into “just another cognitive domain,” will actually set back the cause of understanding complex emotion-cognition interactions instead of advancing it. This applies, for example, to critical processes “on the border,” such as shame and guilt, which reflect complex admixtures of separation distress (the underlying prototype emotional state) and internalized dynamic images of self and other. Shame and guilt are surely more complex than simple separation distress, but at the same time they are clearly more than cognized representations of self and other in interaction (Watt, in press). As pivotal developmental and clinical issues, they are wonderful examples of the true complexity of the cognition-emotion border. From these considerations, I worry that collapsing closely related and deeply interactive, but still in many respects separate, phenomena may not always be the best strategy.

Oliver Turnbull

Oliver Turnbull

Oliver Turnbull  

Dreaming, Deception, and Affective Synaesthesia

Langleben, D. D., Schroeder, L., Maldjian, J. A., Gur, R. C., McDonald, S., Ragland, J. D., O'Brien, C. P., & Childress, A. R. (2002). Brain activity during simulated deception: An event-related functional magnetic resonance study.NeuroImage, 15: 727-732.

There is a long-standing history of interest in methods of identifying deception—including Freud's famous claim that “If his lips are silent, he chatters with his fingertips; betrayal oozes out of him at every pore” (1905, p. 78). More quantifiable approaches for identifying lying might appear to have been developed with the polygraph methods of a few decades ago, but that method is usually not regarded as very reliable. However, a new approach to the problem is suggested by the finding that lying activates, consistently, a series of brain regions that can be tracked using fMRI. On a Guilty Knowledge Test, participants were asked to fire a toy gun and then were scanned while they lied about having fired the shot. Control subjects were treated in the same way but did not shoot the gun. The liars and truth-tellers were readily identified in scans, which identified strong group differences in a range of key brain regions: the anterior cingulate cortex, the superior frontal gyrus, and the left premotor, motor, and anterior parietal cortex. These areas showed higher activation when subjects lied, perhaps consistent with the fact that inhibition of the correct or truthful response may be the key component of the process of deception. Of course, it seems unlikely that we will see such technology deployed in airport security, but the method certainly offers a useful way of investigating the many psychiatric conditions in which deception is a factor. From an analytic perspective, it also offers the possibility of investigating not only such instances of intentional deception, but also the biological basis of unintentional deception—of the sort seen when humans manage to convince ourselves of the merits of an untrue position.

The cognitive Freud

At three meetings during the fall of 2004 the group has centered its discussions on the theories of thought within the Freudian model of the unconscious. We started from Freud's “Formulations on the Two Principles of Mental Functioning”(1911) and compared it to new developments in cognitive neuroscience, such as the works of Westen and Gabbard (2002a, 2002b). One issue relates to the question of the existence of multiple unconscious processes. The following are some of the steps in our reasoning:

The starting point is Freud's idea that the major part of our psychic life is unconscious and that by this proposition Freud pioneered an attempt to direct psychoanalysis toward a natural science.

We are in agreement with Bucci's (2000) affirmation that the Freudian proposition of the models of the mind is in itself a cognitive revolution.

A central thesis states that ideas, feelings, and thoughts are “distributed” in neuronal networks and that they have a tendency to associate with one another.

James Deutsch and Iréne Matthis

Iréne Matthis

email: j.deutsch@utoronto.ca.

Iréne Matthis  

Our group continues to explore psychological trauma from different angles, in an attempt to integrate psychoanalytic and neuroscientific observations and concepts. Recently we have explored this topic via neural networks, psychoanalytic theory of mental processes, and cortical and subcortical memory mechanisms.

How does the brain deal with sudden, unplanned events? On 15 January 2005, Elan Ohayon, of the University of Toronto Epilepsy Research Program, spoke on “Activity Initiation at the Boundaries of Neural and Social Networks.” Freud attempted neural-network models to explain the progression of mental functioning to more complex and sophisticated levels, which are less perturbable by outside influences. Epilepsy researchers are also seeking network models to account for observed clinical phenomena. Seizures can be seen as a “default” state of a network, which interacts with itself, progressing from state to state. Yet most of us do not experience seizures, which thus reflects the complexity and layering of our own central nervous systems. Computer modelling involves simplification, but it is impressive and thought-provoking to “watch” networks “behaving” on the computer screen. Units on the edges of two-dimensional neural arrays, in contrast to those in the middle of the array, which interact with more units, can have a marked influence over the entire network. There was a discussion of possible implications for the psychological sphere, adjusting various types of traumatic influences (sudden overwhelming events without prior warning) on the individual and on the social group.

On 5 March 2005, Dr. Joseph Fernando, President of the Toronto Psychoanalytic Society, presented “More Principles

of Mental Functioning.” Starting from Freud's early and later works outlining the pleasure-unpleasure and reality principles, he discussed some of the confusions regarding more primitive mental functioning, generally involved in traumatic, overwhelming situations. While there can be superficial similarities between these states and primary process (e.g., a sense of timelessness), the more primitive states can be characterized as frozen and fragmented, “everything in pieces.” Trauma may unleash primal defenses (basic defensive maneuvers, as opposed to effective ego-generated mechanisms) rather than an ego regression per se. There is a developmental line from diffuse vegetative excitation to true affect. The more recent term, “mentalization,” may not add usefully to the terms already available. The compulsion to repeat is a clinically prevalent phenomenon and can be seen as a component of the overall primitive response, which, however, may, in later stages of recovery, indicate resumed ego functioning and the reestablishing of the pleasure-unpleasure principle.

Report on the Sixth International Neuro-Psychoanalysis Congress, Rio de Janeiro, 24-27 July 2005

Rita Hayes

Rita Hayes

Brisbane

Rita Hayes  

This Sixth Congress was the first to be held in South America, where there is much interest in the field. Also, for the first time, the Congress preceded the International Psychoanalytical Association Congress—producing some interesting synchrony. The setting, along Copacabana Beach, was stunning. The international mix of delegates was inspiring, with many familiar faces and some new ones, too.

As in previous years, prior to the Congress there was an Educational Day, introduced by Maggie Zellner, and this orientated me and prepared me for the main event. Oliver Turnbull gave an overview of the physiology of sleep and dreaming, Lev Gertsik (California) gave an introduction to the neurochemistry and pharmacology of psychosis, and Howard Shevrin reviewed empirical findings from dream research. The talks reviewed a number of interesting effects—for example, as a feminist I was interested to learn that the content of women's dreams has changed as gender roles have changed. I was also reminded of findings that stress how we often forget our animality. Coming from a child-protection background, I was interested in neuro-psychoanalytic research that looks at animals that eat or smother their young, and its application to maternal ambivalence and aggression in our own species.

Yoram Yovell's historical review of clinical approaches to psychosis did a very good job of surveying a complex field, showing that there is no universally accepted definition of psychosis and that it can occur as part of many psychiatric, neurological, and general medical syndromes (where schizophrenia is merely the most severe and chronic psychotic disorder), and also the fact that schizophrenia, as currently defined by DSM-IV-TR operational criteria, is not one but several related disorders. It was also useful to have a review of the role of different dopamine pathways (mesolimbic vs. mesocortical) in the dichotomy between positive and negative symptoms.

On this first evening we attended a convivial welcome reception at the elegant Copacabana Palace.

Commentary on “Integrating the Psychoanalytic and Neurobiological Views of Panic Disorder”

Robert Cancro

Robert Cancro

New York

Robert Cancro  

Integrating Views of Panic Disorder

There have been two great revolutions in modern psychiatry. The first was the psychoanalytic and the second was the psychopharmacologic. The psychoanalytic was purely mentalist in its approach. Nevertheless, it followed a very traditional mode of science. You observed phenomena, and then you developed theories so as to explain those phenomena. Freud, in particular, was a very keen observer and a very imaginative theoretician who offered internally consistent explanations for the phenomena he observed. The major scientific deficit was that the vast majority of the theoretical formulations were not refutable and others could not even be put to an independent test. “Validation” seemed to come only from the couch, and this is not scientifically sufficient.

Nevertheless, at around the time of World War I, laboratory work was done on subliminal perception which tended to support the hypothesis that a great deal of active mental functioning went on beneath the level of consciousness. Unfortunately, very little additional independent testing of the hypotheses has occurred since the work on subliminal perception. The danger of the psychoanalytic approach is that it can become shared misunderstandings that cannot be refuted. The fact that patients improve is not sufficient validation of either the theory or the practice.

In recent years, there has been a greater emphasis on psychoanalytic treatment as a process of unlearning and relearning. In this model, the intense, safe relationship permits the individual to become more open to looking at the conditions surrounding earlier adaptations and to offer newer ways of dealing with the problems of living. The authors state that early traumatic experiences are stored in the amygdala and that reactivation through talk therapy can ameliorate the effect of those early memories. This point is elaborated upon later in this review.

The psychopharmacologic revolution has at times emphasized biology in a manner that is reductionistic. In a very real sense, the two revolutionary camps have become somewhat overzealous and have difficulty communicating with each other, let alone appreciating what each has to offer. They authors are to be commended for making an attempt to create a truce between these frequently warring camps.

Commentary on “Integrating the Psychoanalytic and Neurobiological Views of Panic Disorder”

Scott Rauch , Mohammed Milad , Carl Marci , Joshua Roffman and Roger Pitman

Roger Pitman

Charlestown, MA

Roger Pitman  

Fear Conditioning Models and Psychoanalysis: from Theory to Treatment

It is a Herculean task to integrate psychoanalytic theory and practice with contemporary neuroscience. In their paper, Alexander, Feigelson, & Gorman attempt to advance such an integration by reconciling the psychoanalytic perspective on panic disorder with a proposed model of fear conditioning as it relates to anxiety disorders. The authors succeed in providing a provocative article that makes accessible current scientific knowledge about fear conditioning and extinction processes while also carefully selecting illustrative examples from psychoanalytic doctrine. In the current commentary, we address several issues that we believe are especially germane to this enterprise.

We propose that it is essential to distinguish between psychoanalytic theory as it relates to the etiology or pathogenesis of psychopathology and the theory and practice of psychoanalysis as a treatment. Contemporary psychoanalytic theory regarding development and emergence of panic disorder (or other “neuroses”) hinges on the idea that key archetypal events in childhood leave residua that remain unresolved and that underpin subsequent emergence of psychopathology. The general idea that early social experiences, especially with parents and primary caregivers, represent critical moments in character development or precipitate vulnerability to the development of psychopathology is not controversial. Certainly, as outlined in the authors' article, the emergence of neuroscience data supporting some of the specific mechanisms that mediate these phenomena in animals is one of the most exciting areas in contemporary neuroscience. However, because they lack an evidentiary basis, assertions of psychoanalytic theory regarding specific events in childhood, and how they are perpetuated and played out in adulthood, have failed to gain acceptance among the broader scientific community. Indeed, inferences from data gathered in adulthood—whether it be retrospective historical information or cross-sectional behavioral phenomena—may not provide a reliable index of childhood experience as it relates to these questions. Hence, the challenge to psychoanalytic theory regarding the etiology and pathogenesis of panic disorder and other neuroses requires the formulation of discrete testable hypotheses (which are still lacking) that almost certainly will need to be tested via longitudinal research designs, conducted beginning in early childhood. In parallel, one can imagine tandem developmental longitudinal efforts to investigate the relationships among genetics, brain structure and function, physiological capacities such as fear conditioning and extinction, temperament or personality structure, attachment styles, and psychopathology. We submit that genes and environment essentially govern brain structure and function, which mediate conditionability and extinction capacity, which in turn largely dictate relevant aspects of personality structure or temperament and hence vulnerability to develop anxiety disorders, such as panic disorder.

years. Since the beginning of 2005 we have been studying affects with the objective of integrating psychoanalysis and neuroscience. This report provides a summary of the relation between anxiety, emotional development, and genetic factors associated with anxiety disorders. A recent article by Gross and Hen, published in Nature Reviews Neuroscience(2004), was taken as a reference point, with the aim of finding a relationship with the Freudian model of “comple-mental series,” as an example of the etiological factor in all mental illness.

From a bibliographic search of The Concordance of the Standard Edition (Guttman, Jones, & Parrish, 1980), we observed that throughout his work, Freud referred to anxiety in no fewer than 125 entries under the heading of affect, showing different aspects of the subject. Summing up briefly, we found it to be important that anxiety, for Freud, was an affect suffered by the ego. It reveals itself as unpleasure, when faced with an unknown object. It produces a fear of being destroyed or harmed by an internal or external force. This brief definition in some way supports the concepts expressed by Gross and Hen. They consider anxiety to be a mental state that is elicited in anticipation of a potential threat or danger. According to these authors, there are abnormal development factors that explain the origin of anxiety. This affect can be understood as being the result of individual traits, which interact with genetic factors and early environmental experience—something similar to that which Freud (1917) studied in the “complemental series” as a constitutional factor plus experiences during infancy. Gross et al. highlight a study in which homozygotic individuals with s/s alleles for the gene that controls the synthesis of the serotonine transporter (5HTT) and which therefore has less efficient neurotransmission (serotonin remains longer in the synaptic space, paradoxically the same as happens when fluoxetine is used in the treatment of depression or anxiety disorders) and therefore has higher scores in anxiety-measurement scales. Under some of the headings in the personality questionnaire (NEO), the scores are higher for the neuroticism dimension and lower for agreeableness. A similar result on the anxiety scales was seen in infants that carry the s/s genotype of the 5HTT gene promoter site. The hypothesis to be considered would be that the inadequate physiology of the serotonergic neurotransmission induces a state of central hyperexcitability mediated by serotonin circuitry. It is surprising that this defect should be similar to the action mechanism of S SRI drugs used to treat anxiety disorders. It is considered that at least for a moment in prenatal development, the opposite effect is necessary to that produced by the SSRI for the appropriate integration of the circuits that control neuronal excitability. These factors would explain why the use of SSRI is not recommended in children. The result of genetic polymorphisms that affect neurotransmission systems do not appear to be definitive if an enriched environment that provides sufficiently good developmental experiences is taken into account.

Introduction: Bulletin 13

Initiating and sustaining studies and research within the new interdisciplinary fields of neuro-psychoanalysis and neuro-psychosomatics is a process fraught with all the ups and downs that attach to every human activity. Some endeavors run into trouble, while others proliferate and breed. Thus the end of 2004 saw the birth of a third group in Brazil: the Neuro-Psychoanalysis Study and Research Group of Rio de Janeiro (GENPSA-Rio). Three additional groups have also been started elsewhere: by Rita Hayes in Brisbane, Australia; by Slawomir Murawiec in Poland; and by Knut Leseth in Bergen, Norway. They are all most heartily welcome.

From some groups there are short messages. Fernando Morena, from the Mexican group, tells me that their time and work has been devoted to the National Psychoanalytic Congress in Mexico City, held in November 2005, with the main topic being Neuroscience and Psychoanalysis. In Finland the original study group, under Turo Reenkola, are in the process of examining closely Freud's 1895 “Project,” and two groups of therapists from Helsingin Psykoterapiayhdistys are studying Jaak Panksepp's Affective Neuroscience.

From Sweden we can report that the group on Philosophy of Psychology are trying to distinguish between reading Kant as an eighteenth-century philosopher and as a psychologist, and they have been discussing the philosophical (epistemological) problems in the writings of Mark Solms and Donald Davidson. The Infant Development group has finished their reading of Fonagy et al., Affect Regulation, Mentalization, and the Development of the Self, and is continuing with more papers on the same topic. The PAPS (Psychoanalytic Psychosomatics) group have used the year 2005 to study psychoanalytic aspects of different somatic illnesses, in order to prepare for a full week (October 17-22) of seminars in Buenos Aires, at the Weizsäcker Centre for Medical Studies. We were invited to this First Argentina-Sweden Encounter by the Fundacíon Luis Chiozza. In the next issue of Neuro-Psychoanalysis, you will have a full report of this meeting.

Report on the Fifth International Neuro-Psychoanalysis Congress, Rome, 2-5 September 2004

Marianne Robert

Marianne Robert

Paris

Marianne Robert  

This year's Congress, on “Splitting, Denial, and Narcissism: Neuro-Psychoanalytic Perspectives on the Right Hemisphere,” took place at the Catholic University of the Sacred Heart in Rome. As in previous years, it was preceded by an Educational Day, this time on the anatomy and physiology of the right hemisphere. It is always most interesting to attend this day, as it reviews a number of basic concepts in the field—which can be very useful for the later parts of the meeting.

This year the Education Day reviewed the findings on the right hemisphere and concrete space, “real” objects, and global processing, and on left-hemisphere abilities relating to more abstract space and linear processing. Also reviewed was that anosognosia (after Babinski) results from pathology of patients with a right-hemisphere lesion, who are often unable to perceive the contralateral space around them and so neglect their left-side hemiplegia. We have learned through recent research that while perception was thought to be the cause of this neglect, there are emotional factors involved as well.

It was interesting to hear during the Education Day about some of the flaws underpinning the oft-cited claim that the right side of the brain is the seat of the system unconscious. Rather, it appears that patients having suffered from lesions in the right hemisphere specifically fail to mourn the lost object, regressing to the part-object. The object is denied, split, projected—presumably because the right hemisphere is where the relation with the whole object is found.

On the first day of the main meeting, Guido Gainotti spoke of his work on the neuropsychological relationship between emotion, unconscious processes, and the right hemisphere—reviewing the claims that the right hemisphere is mainly involved with negative emotional feelings, while the left side of the brain is the home of positive emotions.

Todd Feinberg gave a wonderful presentation on the right hemisphere and the self. He talked about asomatognosia, confabulation, and the Capgras and the Fregoli syndromes. For example, he described the fascinating case of a middle-aged woman who suffered a right-hemisphere lesion and who believes that her reflection in the mirror is a persecuting double, a person who imitates her and wants to harm her. He compared this pathology with that of the Capgras (impostor, or double) syndrome. Other patients with right-hemisphere lesions confabulate, believing their left arm to be a baby, or projecting their pathology onto the patient in the next bed, using splitting, denial, and projection as defense mechanisms with wish-fulfilment. Thus their body image is, somehow, “intact.

Commentary on “Integrating the Psychoanalytic and Neurobiological Views of Panic Disorder”

Katherine Shear

Katherine Shear

Pittsburgh

Katherine Shear  

Psychoanalytic Ideas in Modern Psychiatric Practice

Alexander, Feigelson, & Gorman embark on an intellectually precarious journey in attempting to unite vastly dissimilar realms of inquiry that are both temporally and conceptually distant. The paper describing this effort demonstrates an impressive breadth of knowledge and an underlying generosity of spirit; however, the enterprise is too ambitious to succeed. The authors are trying to link nineteenth-century Freudian ideas to developing twenty-first-century neurobiological models of panic, using results of twentieth-century fear-conditioning experiments as a bridge. Neither psychoanalysis nor neuroscience is sufficiently well specified for such an enterprise. Conditioning experiments have provided interesting data, but a great deal is still unknown about fear conditioning, especially in humans. To provide just a few examples, there is some evidence that conditioned learning in infants follows different principles from those in adults. When and how do such differences occur across the lifespan? How does fear learning interact with specific contextual variables, such as the state of the attachment system? How does the attachment system work? There are many such unresolved questions, so it is premature to create an integrated model using fear conditioning as its bedrock.

While psychoanalysts theorize about normal psychological functioning, they do not engage in intensive observation of normal behavior. Instead, this group concerns itself with a theory of the mind developed from observations in the consulting-room. In the case of this paper, the observations of Freud himself play a central role, mostly unmodified by late twentieth-century work. Neuroscientists work in a very different way. Investigation pertains to studying properties of specific brain functions. Research is carried out primarily by nonclinical scientists, and investigators use accumulating answers to specific questions in order to develop provisional models of how the brain works. The object of inquiry is as likely to be a nonhuman animal or a normal human control as a clinically ill patient. Moreover, neuroscience is in its infancy. We do not yet understand how the brain works. Fear-conditioning research is a subset of neuroscience study that has been underway for many decades. This work uses experimental paradigms and is most often conducted in small mammals. Thus there are vast differences between psychoanalysis and neurobiology with respect to questions that are asked, the way of obtaining knowledge, the subjects who are studied, and the process of developing explanatory models. It is not clear that findings or ideas from one group can be easily translated to the other.

A Paradox of Studying Dream Alteration in Patients with Pontine Lesions

Calvin Yu

Calvin Yu

Hong Kong

Calvin Yu  

The activation-synthesis hypothesis of dreaming attempted to replace the Freudian theory with a brain-based model. According to this classical model, the conscious experience of dreaming involves an interplay between excitatory and inhibitory neurons in the pons. Recent research has cast doubt on this classical hypothesis by demonstrating that pontine lesions do not lead to a cessation of dreaming, implying that the pons may be unnecessary for dreaming. However, scrupulous human lesion studies are required in order to clarify the role of the pons in dreaming. Three case examples with lesions to various brainstem regions are reported in this paper to illustrate the paradox and difficulties of carrying out pontine-lesion studies.

Commentary on “Becoming Aware of Feelings”

Arnold Modell

Arnold Modell

Boston

Arnold Modell  

Being aware of feelings both in ourselves and in our patients is an essential aspect of the practice of psychoanalysis. Psychoanalysts have therefore acquired a huge clinical data base concerning the phenomenology of feelings. This accumulated experience of over 100 years of clinical observation has provided psychoanalysts with a sophisticated and complex knowledge of emotions and feelings. This has occurred despite the fact that psychoanalysis does not yet possess an adequate theory of affects. Psychoanalysts observe not only the emotional upheavals of transference but also an entire range of defenses against the emergence of feelings. These observations need to be grounded in a neurobiology of emotion and feeling, but what psychoanalysts can learn from cognitive science must also be consonant with their own hard-won clinical knowledge.

When I attempt to synthesize this clinical knowledge with the research findings of cognitive scientists, which Lane & Garfield have summarized, I am made uneasy and experience a feeling of conceptual dissonance. I recognize that there are basic assumptions, concerning the relation of consciousness to the unconscious mind, that separate me from cognitive science. This is illustrated in cognitive science's assumption of a “procedural” unconscious that is devoid of meaning. Furthermore, much of this target paper consists of reports of certain experiments of cognitive scientists that I believe have very little relevance for psychoanalysis. I see this as a problem of context—that feelings generated in the experimental procedures of cognitive science cannot easily be analogized to feelings that are generated within the psychoanalytic setup.

Arnold H. Modell, M.D.: Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School at Beth Israel Hospital, Boston, MA, U.S.A.

Commentary on “Becoming Aware of Feelings”

Michael Posner

Michael Posner

Eugene

Michael Posner  

Development of Self-Regulation

Richard Lane and David Garfield present a well-reasoned analysis of research on brain mechanisms underlying conscious awareness of emotion. There could hardly be a topic of greater centrality to psychoanalysis. They do an excellent job in conveying the exciting findings and methods of cognitive neuroscience to a broad community interested in understanding the neural basis for emotional awareness.

Basic to psychoanalysis are Freud's ideas concerning how cognitive and affective control develops from the primary process of early infancy. On these issues of development, Lane & Garfield are relatively silent. In a section on the topic of “speculation on self-regulation,” they cite imaging studies showing that when attempting to ward off arousal from a sexual stimulus or negative emotion from pictorial input, adults show increased activity in a neural network including the anterior cingulate gyrus. Their idea is that the cingulate is part of a neural network involved in regulating the emotions. There is good evidence (Bush, Luu, & Posner, 2000) that separate areas of the cingulate serve to regulate both emotions and cognitions and that this circuitry is a critical part of an executive attention network that develops strongly in early and middle childhood (see Fig. 1).

Michael I. Posner: Department of Psychology, University of Oregon, Eugene, Oregon, U.S.A.

The Brisbane Group held its inaugural meeting on 11 April 2005. It was attended by 37 professionals from diverse backgrounds, but predominantly psychologists and social workers. The group meets monthly and has a basic three-year plan. The first year has been devoted to acquiring a sufficient grasp of the neuroscience concepts and a vocabulary essential for a critical reading of some of the relevant literature. Thus prepared, the second year will be devoted to working through some of the significant recent neuroscience and neuro-psychoanalytic literature that is of direct relevance to professionals working in the areas of infant mental health, early development and trauma, and child protection. By the third year we expect to have a sufficient foundation to develop our own research ideas and projects, which will be predominantly practitioner-based. Our format for the first year was a video-showing of Mark Solms's lectures on “The Brain for Beginners,” followed by discussions based also on extracts from The Brain and the Inner World (Solms & Turnbull, 2002). We plan to continue with the works of Jaak Panksepp, Allan N. Schore, Peter Fonagy, and others. Our focus and long-term aim is prevention: where prevention fails, the development of effective evidence-based and cost-effective, treatment guidelines is important

It is our intention that the study group should function as a peer support group and also encourage and support members who wish to undertake their own research. It will provide a secure base for the exploration of ideas and the development of a professional practice that is evidence-based. It is important to us that the group be as inclusive as possible, having the widest possible composition and representing as many professions as possible. We expect that numbers may drop as we move beyond the educational phase of the first year, but we feel this educational function to be vital in terms both of providing ourselves with secure foundations and of providing much-sought-after professional development for the community at large.

The Impact of Defensive Denial upon Adjustment Following Traumatic Brain Injury

Tamara Ownsworth

Tamara Ownsworth

St Lucia, Australia

Tamara Ownsworth  

Individuals with a highly defensive personality style tend to present themselves in an overly favorable light and deny personal inadequacies. Following traumatic brain injury (TBI), denial may be an adaptive strategy to protect individuals from the overwhelming reality of their situation. However, persisting denial can interfere with the adjustment process and hinder the development of more adaptive coping strategies. A case study is presented of JK, a 45-year-old woman with a highly defensive personality style, who sustained a TBI. JK developed social anxiety and depression and was referred for psychological support following a progressive deterioration in her overall functioning. The treatment program was based on an individual-psychotherapy approach, with generalization of skills in a group-therapy setting. A comparison of preand posttreatment functioning indicated a significant reduction in her level of social anxiety, depression, defensiveness, and functional impairment. Independent neuropsychological assessments, conducted for medico-legal purposes, prior to and following the intervention, indicated a significant improvement in JK's cognitive performance between periods of testing. The implications of this study are discussed in terms of the impact of defensive denial upon postinjury adjustment and therapeutic approaches.

Commentary on “Integrating the Psychoanalytic and Neurobiological Views of Panic Disorder”

Andrew Aronson

Andrew Aronson

New York

Andrew Aronson  

Oedipus Notwithstanding

What frightens us? Alexander, Feigelson, & Gorman have summarized the neurobiology of fear and cogently argued for the homology of these fear mechanisms with those of anxiety generally and panic disorder specifically. Their central thesis explicates a phenomenology of learned behavior in the pathogen-esis of panic, which has been advanced in the service of the ambitious and laudable goal of integrating neurobiological and psychoanalytic theory, at least as pertains to this condition. In some aspects finely woven tapestry, in other aspects patchwork quilt, their thesis offers a trove of ideas and questions to contemplate in regard to the potential integration of these ostensibly different domains. The hard science that stands in support of at least some of their thesis presents a useful challenge to psychoanalytic theorists to integrate its discrete findings, if not its speculations, which are far more plentiful. Indeed, psychoanalytic theorists cannot ignore the findings of neuroscience, and the field should welcome opportunities, however tentative, for integration. To be sure and to be clear, we are still at the level of comparing theoretical models, not reconciling and integrating data.

As presented in the paper, evidence from both animal and human models compellingly argues for a biology of fear and anxiety expressed as a learned and thereby enduring response. The anxiety response is potentially evoked by a universe of triggers increasingly populated by life experience—a response that can also be, must also be, unlearned to secure any remedy. It bears emphasis that this model posits an actual experience of danger, inextricably coupled with an adaptive fear response occurring in the earliest eras of precognitive development, as a predicate to the later experience of panic. When later occurring apart from objective danger, panic is considered archaic and maladaptive, a response insufficiently mediated (inhibited) by reason—that is, the prefrontal cortex. Though largely based in the study of nonhuman animals, the science of this model extends into the elucidation of relevant brain neurocircuits required to manifest a fear response, and yet further into identification of the relevant molecules and cells involved in the acquisition, maintenance, and control of fear memory. It is a model that disposes well to conceptualization of the clinical findings of the often exquisite and frequently escalating vulnerability of those affected by panic disorder, to an understanding of chronicity, and to strategies for therapeutic modification. These are ideas of powerful promise and prospect.

Emotional Memory, Trust, and Hypnotic Suggestion.

Adolphs, R., Tranel, D., & Buchanan, T. W. (2005). Amygdala damage impairs emotional memory for gist but not details of complex stimuli.Nature Neuroscience, 8: 512-518.

We have long known two rather independent facts, in diverse fields, that are brought together in this interesting paper. First, in neuroscience we know that the amygdala is involved in several aspects of emotion, most notably as regards the memory of events (especially fearful situations). Second, in clinical psychology, we have also long known that patients with mental health problems have difficulty recalling specific aspects of their previous life experience: some (for example, in depression) seem especially impaired in recalling gist rather than detail, while the converse is true for other states (those of an anxious or traumatic nature). This latter finding is especially important for psychoanalysis and related psychotherapies because so much of the therapeutic experience is mediated by the ability of the client to consciously recall his or her life experiences and to place them in a coherent narrative. The findings of Adolphs et al. bring together these two strands and allow us to better understand the role of emotion in the reexperiencing of a personal narrative in studies of patients with focal lesions to the amygdala and related structures. The patients are asked to recall images that may be neutral (a car ride for relaxation) or emotionally valenced (a car ride to recover the body of a dead child), with later questions about gist (e.g., who are the characters in the image) or details (background specifics, such as cloud formations). The findings show that the amygdala seems to be central for the recall of gist, while the hippocampus is critical for the recall of detail—with selective loss of each category after selective lesions. We also know that powerful affective experiences are associated with enormous changes in hormones, such as cortisol, that modify the ability of brain regions such as the amygdala and hippocampus to lay down memories—which goes some way to explaining the fact that events experienced in powerful affective states (such as trauma) produce good gist information, but poor recall of detail.

[[RunningHead]]

Emotions, Unconscious Processes, and the Right Hemisphere

Guido Gainotti

Guido Gainotti

Rome

Guido Gainotti  

Since the classical Babinski's (1914) observation of lack of awareness (“anosognosia“) for a left-sided hemiplegia, the problem of the mechanisms underlying this surprising phenomenon has been raised. Most authors have stressed the links between right hemisphere and emotional processes, considering anosognosia as an abnormal emotional reaction, caused by disruption of the side of the brain crucially involved in emotional behavior. Theoretically motivated models of hemispheric asymmetries in emotional processing have proposed either a right-hemisphere dominance for specific components of emotions, or a different involvement of the right and left hemispheres in different levels of emotional processing. Following the last line of thought, we have proposed that the right hemisphere may subserve the lower “schematic” level (where emotions are automatically generated and experienced as “true emotions) and the left hemisphere the higher “conceptual” level (where emotions are consciously analyzed and submitted to an intentional control). In agreement with this model, recent empirical data strongly suggest that the right hemisphere might play a major role in the automatic, unconscious generation of emotions, whereas the left hemisphere could be mainly involved in the conscious analysis and control of emotional processes.

Jaak Panksepp

Jaak Panksepp

Bowling Green, Ohio

Jaak Panksepp  

On the Primal Nature of Affective Consciousness: What are the Relations Between Emotional Awareness and Affective Experience?

Prefatory note: This commentary has been revised after extensive discussions with Richard Lane. Coming from somewhat different intellectual-research traditions, my original commentary contained various misunderstandings of their position, and their paper of mine. We enjoyed some detailed discussion about various disagreements before we were finally on the same page. Through our private discussions, we have reached a better understanding of the different ways we use some concepts and have resolved some disagreements that prevented us from seeing eye to eye. By agreement with Lane and Garfield, I will be happy to provide an electronic version of that text to interested readers (jpankse@bgnet.bgsu.edu). This can provide an extended subtext that can allow readers to appreciate the conceptual complexities that all too often make productive communication across disciplinary boundaries a challenge. It may serve as a model for how needless controversy can be reduced without losing substantive issues that need to be discussed further.

Lane & Garfield provide a wide-ranging critical analysis of the importance of emotional awareness in psychiatric and psychoanalytic practice. They summarize their important psychometric tools to monitor the degree of emotional self-awareness and the brain changes that accompany mild states of emotional arousal. Their work highlights the importance of humans becoming cognitively aware of their affective states, and the utility of this information for clinical practice. I agree with most of their points, and the utility of their approaches for a neuro-psychoanalytic science. However, I believe that a key element of human affectivity, probably shared homologously by all mammals, has been underemphasized. Perhaps they can elaborate on their views about the neurobiological nature of the many basic affective states human can experience—in my estimation, a primary-process form of phenomenal consciousness—and how we can ever scientifically understand how affects are actually generated in the brain/mind. It does not seem that their LEAS scale, nor modern brain imaging, are optimally designed to get at such issues.

Elusive Illusions

Reality Judgment and Reality Assignment in Dreams and Waking Life

Mark Blechner

Mark Blechner

New York

Mark Blechner  

This paper presents some proposals about the nature of reality monitoring during sleep and its neurobiological basis. An example of a dream from a psychoanalytic treatment is described in which the dreamer saw his deceased father alive. The dreamer judged in the dream that he had fantasized this before, but in the dream, “this was real.” This example is used to explore several questions: (1) To what degree are the reality-monitoring systems of dreaming and waking unitary or separate? (2) Is “reality” a property of experience that is perceived or assigned? (3) How do affective considerations shape our perception or assignment of reality? (4) Does death of a loved one have a special capacity to modify reality judgments? Finally, (5) what can we learn from neurological data about these psychological phenomena? Data from neuropsychological studies of many types are cited that implicate frontal limbic areas, especially the anterior cingulate, in the process of distinguishing fantasy, dream, and waking reality.

Psychobiological Theories of Panic Attacks and Panic Disorders

Alexander, Feigelson, & Gorman entertain a fear-conditioning model of panic disorders that seeks to integrate first-person experiential views and third-person neuroscientific approaches in a seamless synthesis. It is not yet clear to me what specific testable hypotheses arise from their perspective. May I request the authors to advance a few? For my part I shall simply supplement their coverage with a more comprehensive summary of current neuroscientific possibilities for understanding panic attacks.

Perhaps a clearer distinction between panic attacks and panic disorders will be critical for how well Gorman, Kent, Sullivan, and Coplan's (2000) amygdala-based fear system model of panic will hold up to empirical scrutiny. At this point, a critical issue is to clarify how the precipitous affective surges of panic emerge from brain dynamics, along with an explicit recognition that the affective sources of acute panic attacks may be quite different from the anticipatory “signal anxiety” that eventually culminates in the chronic panic syndrome.

[[RunningHead]]

Passivity Phenomena

Implications for the Concept of Self

Ralf-Peter Behrendt

Ralf-Peter Behrendt

York, U.K.

Ralf-Peter Behrendt  

Philosophers and theoretical psychologists have in the past tried to elucidate the nature of self, volition, and agency from a fundamental position of determinism. Although the idea that we are driven to action by instincts has fallen out of favor in an age of cognitive psychology and information-processing paradigms of the mind, deterministic approaches predicted principles of the organization of voluntary behavior that can now successfully integrate psychological and neuroanatomical data. Motor acts (and thoughts) form part of a “total performance” in that they serve as tools for higher-level drives and motivations. At the same time, there is evidence to suggest that dispositions to actions (and thoughts) are induced by perceived events or objects-consistent with behaviorism—and that the actualization of these dispositions is promoted or inhibited by currently prevailing drives. The organization of the basal ganglia-thalamocortical system normally ensures that only those response tendencies are acted upon that are consistent with the organism's current drive state. It is argued here that drive reduction experienced in conjunction with the perception of our movements and thoughts is responsible for the sense of self-generation, or “coming from me,” which is characteristic of our actions and thoughts, and that, when dispositions to such actions and thoughts are excited by environmental or “inner” stimuli in a manner that defies prevailing drives, passivity experiences can arise.

The Instinctual Basis of Human Affect

Affective and fMRI Imaging of Laughter and Crying

Nakia Gordon , Jaak Panksepp , Michael Dennis and John McSweeny

John McSweeny

John McSweeny  

To investigate whether affective experience is linked to the neurodynamics of basic emotional systems, a novel mood-induction procedure was utilized to induce affective changes and observe the neural consequences. The internal motor imagery of laughter and crying (to evoke joy and sadness), along with the affectively neutral task of walk imagery, allowed evocation of affective states without the confounding effects of motor artifacts. Affective response scores (nine-point Likert scale) indicated that internal laughter significantly increased happiness and decreased sadness. Conversely, crying imagery significantly increased sadness and decreased happiness. Seven brain regions exhibited BOLD signal changes in the emotion tasks, which were not observed during the neutral walking task. These regions are the left basal ganglia, right putamen, insula, thalamus, and inferior occipital gyrus, and left and right caudate. These data suggest that there may be a shared neural system for activating affective responses.

Becoming Aware of Feelings

Integration of Cognitive-Developmental, Neuroscientific, and Psychoanalytic Perspectives

Richard Lane and David Garfield

David Garfield

Tucson

North Chicago

David Garfield  

A fundamental ingredient of psychoanalytic treatment is the ability of the analysand to become consciously aware of his or her own emotional responses. We propose that the conscious awareness of emotion is a type of information processing that can be viewed as a separate domain of cognitive function, that the transition from unconscious (implicit) to conscious (explicit) aspects of emotion can be understood developmentally in the manner described by Piaget for cognitive functions generally, and that explicit emotional processes have a modulatory effect on implicit processes. We then present a parallel hierarchical model of the neural substrates of emotional experience supported by recent neuroimaging work. We describe how the neural substrates of implicit and explicit aspects of emotion are dissociable, and we discuss the neural substrates of implicit aspects of emotion, background feelings, focal attention to feelings, and reflective awareness of feelings. This framework constitutes an alternative to traditional psychoanalytic understandings of insight. We conclude by discussing the implications of this model for psychoanalysis, including the nature of clinical change, the psychological processes involved in change with and without insight, and a framework for conceptualizing how to promote emotional change in a variety of clinical settings.

“Daughter-Somatoparaphrenia” in Women with Right-Hemisphere Syndrome

A Psychoanalytic Perspective on Neurological Body Knowledge Disorders

Catherine Morin , Stéphane Thibierge , Pascale Bruguière , Pascale Pradat-Diehl and Dominique Mazevet

Dominique Mazevet

Paris

Dominique Mazevet  

Disorders of discourse and behavior-in particular anosognosia and somatoparaphrenia-may be associated with body schema neurological disorders in the right-hemisphere syndrome (RHS). From a psychoanalytic point of view, the content of the patient's discourse may be considered an alteration of the unified conception an individual has of him/herself—that is, of what Lacan called specular image. After presenting the specificities of the Lacanian conception of specular image, we consider its heuristic value in the RHS field, based on three detailed observations of women with anosognosia and hemineglect. Each of the three patients personified her paralyzed hand as being or belonging to a daughter, whether real or imagined. We propose considering this symptom as a disclosure of the object (in the accepted psychoanalytic meaning of the term) that is normally repressed. We briefly discuss how these observations indirectly shed light on the mind-brain problem.

Jack Gorman

New York

Jack Gorman  

To facilitate cross-talk between current neuroscientific and psychoanalytic views, it is useful to deal with areas of common ground. One such domain is the neural and behavioral basis of anxiety, a relatively well-understood area of study, which has received substantial interest from both neuroscience and psychoanalysis over the years, especially as regards topics such as fear conditioning and uncontrollable anxiety. This paper focuses on the unconscious “learning” processes, which are well-known to psychoanalysis but are also described increasingly in neuroscientific terms. Panic disorder—one of the manifestations of anxiety that has received most attention from both psychoanalytic theory and neuroscience—especially lends itself to scrutiny under the classical conditioning lens. This paper highlights the long work of synthesis that is still required to provide a more complete account that makes both neuroscientific and psychoanalytic sense—but which is ultimately necessary for the future of psychiatry.

This is an ambitious and important attempt to bridge psychoanalysis and the clinical neuroscience of anxiety disorders, and although the title emphasizes panic disorder, Alexander, Feigelson, & Gorman review many other clinical anxiety disorders and offer many fine summaries of literatures. I would say that in general I am quite sympathetic with the overall aims of the authors, but I do feel that a couple of issues might get somewhat better underlined.

The centerpiece of some of these more modest differences with the authors might be a larger emphasis on the primacy of separation distress as a prototype emotion. This tendency toward conflation of the two distinct prototype states of fear versus separation distress and the neglect of separation distress is unfortunately widespread within psychiatry, and it is a principled distinction in terms of a nosology for prototype emotion worth emphasizing at the start (Panksepp, 1998; see Panksepp & Watt, 2003, for further elaborations). The authors start out with classical psychoanalytic theory about the nature of anxiety from the standpoint of a basically energic drive theory, but unfortunately they neglect some less visible strands of Freud's thinking that might relate panic disorders more to separation distress. One of Freud's more insightful statements about anxiety was about how human infant had the challenge of “helpless longing.” This formulation for (separation) anxiety as “helpless longing” was generally lost in mechanistic-hydraulic drive-theory metaphors (“what is the poor undeveloped creature to do with his longing”—Freud, 1927). There is rarely, if ever, a principled distinction drawn in much of the psychiatric literature between separation anxiety and fear as truly distinct emotional systems in the brain.
